title: Moses sees the land (Deuteronomy 34)
hook: on Mount Nebo he sees the land he'll never enter, and dies

segments.voice: Yesterday: choose life, two plates set before a people, and the word close at hand. Your line: near, in your mouth and in your heart.
screen: `NEAR, IN YOUR MOUTH AND IN YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: An old man climbs a mountain. He's a hundred and twenty. Forty of those years he's spent walking a whole people through the desert: complaints and manna, golden calves and giants, the long funeral march of a generation. Now they're camped by the Jordan River, one crossing away from the land. But he won't cross. He's been told. So he climbs Mount Nebo, east of the river, and at the top God shows him everything: the hills to the north, the valleys, the palm-tree city of Jericho, all the way to the sea in the west.
screen: `A HUNDRED AND TWENTY YEARS OLD.` → `ONE RIVER AWAY.` → `UP NEBO, TO SEE.`

segments.voice: Then God says, in the King James Bible: "I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither." Why can't he go? Back in Numbers, at a place called Meribah, Moses struck the rock twice with his rod instead of speaking to it as God told him, and he was told then that he wouldn't lead the people in. Readers still argue about whether that seems fair. The text doesn't argue. "So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab." Then a mysterious detail: he buried him, the text says, in a valley, and tradition reads he as God, "but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day." No grave to visit, no shrine. The people go on without a monument. The chapter adds that "his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated." He didn't wear out. He was simply finished. It ends with an epitaph: there arose not a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face. Who wrote a chapter describing Moses' own death? Jewish tradition, in the Talmud, offers more than one answer: some sages said Joshua wrote the last verses; others said Moses wrote them himself, in tears. Today Mount Nebo is in Jordan, and pilgrims climb it to look out over the same view. Moses gave his whole life to a promise he saw but didn't enter. Christians remember that he does appear, much later, on another mountain, talking with Jesus at the transfiguration.
screen: `SEE IT, BUT NOT GO OVER.` · `NO MAN KNOWETH HIS GRAVE.` · `HIS EYE WAS NOT DIM.` · `WHO WROTE HIS DEATH?` · then, large: `I HAVE CAUSED THEE TO SEE IT WITH THINE EYES.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're working toward that will likely outlast you: children, students, a garden, a cause, a tree you planted. Picture it years from now, flourishing, without you in the picture, and like Moses on the mountain, let it be enough to have seen it begin. If you pray, bless it, and the people who'll carry it on.
Nebo. The mountain east of the Jordan where Moses, at a hundred twenty, saw the promised land he would never enter.
Your line: seeing is enough. The view from Nebo is still there, for anyone who climbs. Rest well.

original.note: Hebrew: Nebo, the mountain east of the Jordan where Moses saw the land. Today it is in Jordan.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad ending.
what it means: a life given to a promise he saw but didn't enter, ending with no grave and an epitaph: no prophet like him.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud debates who wrote the Torah's last verses, Joshua or Moses in tears; and Nebo looks across to Jericho.

chat.says: Moses led everyone for forty years. Why didn't he get to go into the land?
options: At Meribah he struck the rock instead of speaking to it, so he would only see it.
He was afraid of the giants, like the ten spies, and refused to cross.
He chose to stay behind in Egypt to care for the people left there.
chat.meaning: Numbers tells how Moses struck the rock at Meribah instead of speaking to it. On Nebo, God shows him the land: see it, but not go over.

notes: Editor review (y2 days 407–424): fixed "his entire adult life" (Moses was already grown before the forty years); Meribah no longer says "in anger" (Numbers 20 says he struck the rock twice instead of speaking to it); cut "for centuries"; Deuteronomy 34:6 says "he buried him", now told as tradition reading "he" as God; epitaph paraphrase brought closer to 34:10 ("since in Israel"); cut the Pope John Paul II / year 2000 visit (not in the cited text); "alone" dropped from the climb (the text doesn't say it); howItsDone "often" removed.
Bava Batra 15a: one view that Joshua wrote the last eight verses; R. Simeon's view that Moses wrote them in tears (or 'with tears'). Paraphrased; confirm.
Pope John Paul II's March 2000 visit to Mount Nebo was cut in the editor review (date not in the cited text).
Meribah (Numbers 20:7–12): Moses was told to speak to the rock and struck it; the script says 'in anger'. Confirm the characterization.
Deuteronomy 34:6 'he buried him' is often read as God burying Moses; the script says God buried him. Confirm.
